title: A finite-depth annular screen keeps a sharp direct X-ray ingress for 14 cycles despite Kepler shear
abstract: We test whether Kepler shear alone must broaden a recurring X-ray ingress. We compute direct transmission through one circular annular sector with finite radial depth. Extinction along a ray adds before flux is computed. With a radial width of one percent, a grey radial depth of 1,000, and a 108.44-day inner period, all 14 tested cycles retain an 80-to-5-percent ingress of 1.50-1.51 observer days. The half-flux phase shifts by only 0.022 days. The low interval instead grows from 34.15 to 55.30 days. The exact opaque limit links this growth to the difference between outer and inner periods, 1.63066 days per cycle. A finite-depth point-ray formula explains why shear does not set a depth-independent ingress width. This is a prescribed geometry and direct-beam result, not a fit to ASASSN-14ko or a gas survival model. A reference scattering opacity gives a six-solar-mass sector. Pressure, ionization, radiation forces and scattered light can invalidate its use as a physical screen. The result gives a duration test for this family and limits what sharp ingress alone can show.

display.caption: Synthetic direct flux, low intervals and depth dependence for a sheared annular sector. No telescope measurements are plotted.
